item.title: TMJ & Craniofacial — NAG / SNAG Guidance
clinicalUse: Use when assessment identifies a relevant impairment in TMJ & Craniofacial and the parent technique fits the patient's presentation.
Primary treatment target: jaw opening/closing, lateral excursion, chewing tolerance and related craniofacial muscle symptoms.
Retain the technique only if it produces a meaningful within-session improvement.
patientPosition: Supported sitting or supine with the head and neck relaxed.
Keep the jaw in a comfortable resting position before testing or treatment.
therapistPosition: Stand or sit at the head/side with the patient's head fully supported.
Use small, precise contacts; avoid forcing the mandible.
stabilization: Support the cranium and, when needed, stabilize one side of the mandible without compressing the throat.
contact: Use broad, gentle extra-oral contact over the relevant joint or muscle target.
Intra-oral techniques require specific training, infection-control procedures and explicit consent.
Use a trained facet/segmental contact that supports the intended spinal glide.
Self-SNAGs use a towel/belt only after the direction has been taught and reproduced safely.
forceDirection: NAGs use a passive oscillatory glide; SNAGs sustain the glide while the patient actively moves.
The movement should be pain-free or clearly easier.
dosage: Commonly 6–10 repetitions, stopping if symptoms worsen or the pain-free effect is lost.
steps: 1. Record the exact comparable sign for TMJ & Craniofacial: jaw opening/closing, lateral excursion, chewing tolerance and related craniofacial muscle symptoms.
2. Screen regional red flags, contraindications and technique-specific precautions before touching the patient.
3. Position and stabilize the patient so the target is comfortable and the manual input can be localized.
4. Apply a low-force trial using the parent technique principles and the region-specific contact described above.
5. Monitor pain quality, symptom distribution, guarding and patient confidence throughout.
6. Re-test the original comparable sign immediately after the trial.
7. Keep the technique only when the response is useful, then transfer the gain into active movement, loading or self-management.
mistakes: Applying the technique because it is familiar rather than because the examination supports it.
Using more force when the response is unclear or worsening.
Failing to re-test the exact movement or function that justified the treatment.
safety: Avoid aggressive force after acute trauma, suspected fracture/dislocation, active dental infection or unexplained cranial nerve signs.
Stop or modify if symptoms peripheralize, neurological status worsens, the response is disproportionate or the patient asks to stop.
